title: Decompose complex work into accountable tasks
description: Break a broad request into bounded AI tasks, human decisions, dependencies, and review points.
outcome: You can create a task map that uses AI for suitable parts of the work without losing ownership of the whole.
objectives: Separate analysis, drafting, verification, and decision tasks.
Assign an input, output, owner, and acceptance check to each AI-assisted step.
Keep engineering and program decisions at explicit human control points.

concepts.title: Decompose by deliverable
concepts.body: Large requests hide several different jobs. Split them into outputs that can be checked independently, such as an evidence table, open-question list, draft summary, and decision brief.

concepts.title: Mark the seams
concepts.body: Each task should state what enters, what leaves, and who accepts it. Clear seams stop an early model error from silently flowing into later work.
concepts.example: An engineer approves extracted test facts before a program analyst uses them in a schedule-impact draft.

concepts.title: Reserve judgment
concepts.body: AI may organize approved evidence and draft alternatives. Technical authority, contractual interpretation, compliance determinations, and mission decisions stay with authorized people.

practice.title: Turn a broad anomaly request into a reviewable task map
instructions: Read the broad request and identify the separate work products inside it.
Define where AI may assist and where an authorized person must decide.
Compare your map with the success checks and model answer.
practice.scenario: A program manager receives an approved, sanitized thermal-test anomaly summary and asks the team to assess schedule impact. No controlled technical data or customer-sensitive material may enter this training workflow.
practice.starterPrompt: Review this engineering issue, tell us what it means, and recommend what the program should do.

fields.label: Work products
fields.placeholder: Fact table, missing-information list, schedule scenarios, decision brief

fields.label: AI-assistable tasks
fields.prompt: Which bounded tasks can AI support with approved inputs?
fields.placeholder: Extract stated facts, organize dependencies, draft scenario language

fields.label: Human control gates
fields.prompt: Who validates technical meaning and accepts the recommendation?
fields.placeholder: Responsible engineer validates facts; program manager owns schedule decision

fields.label: Acceptance checks
fields.prompt: What must be true before each output moves forward?
fields.placeholder: Every claim traces to the approved summary; uncertainty remains labeled

successChecks: The broad request is divided into independently reviewable outputs.
Every AI task has a limited input and a named acceptance check.
Technical and program decisions have explicit human owners.
The plan does not request or infer controlled technical details.
practice.modelAnswer: 1. AI extracts only stated facts, dates, and open questions from the approved sanitized summary; the responsible engineer validates the table. 2. AI organizes the validated facts into schedule dependency scenarios without selecting a technical disposition; the scheduler checks logic and dates. 3. AI drafts a brief that separates evidence, assumptions, and options; the program manager reviews it with engineering. 4. The authorized technical and program owners decide the disposition and schedule response. Stop if required information is not approved for this tool.

quiz.prompt: What is the strongest reason to split a complex AI workflow into smaller tasks?

options.text: It makes the prompt look more sophisticated.
options.feedback: Appearance is not the goal. The value is control, reviewability, and clearer ownership.

options.text: It creates checkpoints where inputs, outputs, and errors can be inspected.
options.feedback: Correct. Bounded steps make it easier to catch problems before they propagate.

options.text: It removes the need for subject-matter experts.
options.feedback: No. Experts are especially important at technical, contractual, compliance, and mission control points.

quiz.explanation: Decomposition improves control when each step has a clear output, check, and owner.

quiz.prompt: Which task is most appropriate to reserve for an authorized human?

options.text: Formatting validated facts into a table
options.feedback: This is a bounded transformation task that AI may support with approved data and review.

options.text: Generating neutral headings for a draft
options.feedback: This is a low-judgment drafting task, subject to normal review.

options.text: Accepting the technical disposition and program schedule impact
options.feedback: Correct. Accountable technical and program authorities must own these decisions.

quiz.explanation: AI can support the evidence flow, but authority and accountability do not transfer to the model.

quiz.prompt: A downstream summary depends on facts extracted by AI. What should happen first?

options.text: A qualified reviewer validates the extracted facts against the approved source.
options.feedback: Correct. Validate the upstream artifact before it becomes input to another step.

options.text: The next AI step should assume extraction is accurate.
options.feedback: An unchecked error can compound across the workflow.

options.text: Delete the source so the summary becomes authoritative.
options.feedback: The source remains the authority. Provenance should be preserved, not removed.

quiz.explanation: Control at task seams prevents error propagation and preserves traceability.

takeaway: For every AI-assisted step, name the approved input, reviewable output, acceptance check, and accountable human.

title: Design risk-based inputs and permissions
description: Match tools, data, access, and review to the sensitivity and consequence of a defense-contractor workflow.
outcome: You can create an input plan that minimizes exposure and routes uncertain material to the right policy owner.
objectives: Evaluate classification, contract, proprietary, privacy, and export-control signals before use.
Separate tool approval from authorization to use a specific dataset for a specific purpose.
Plan safe alternatives such as public, synthetic, aggregated, or approved reusable content.

concepts.title: Approval has layers
concepts.body: An enterprise AI tool may be approved generally while a particular contract, dataset, or customer use is not. Confirm the tool, data type, purpose, access, and applicable program rules together.

concepts.title: Design the minimum input set
concepts.body: Start with the smallest approved facts that can answer the question. Public references, synthetic examples, and approved reusable capability statements can often support early drafting.

concepts.title: Route, do not interpret
concepts.body: When markings, clauses, handling rules, or ownership are unclear, pause and route the question to Security, Contracts, Legal, Export Compliance, Privacy, or the designated program owner. This course does not provide legal advice.

practice.title: Build a safe source set for a solution brief
instructions: Classify each proposed input for this approved training workflow.
Use the feedback to identify a safer source or required approval.
Assume no material may be reclassified by the learner.
practice.scenario: A solutions and proposals team is drafting a fictional capability brief in an approved business AI environment. Only public and explicitly approved reusable content is in scope.

categories.label: Ready
categories.description: Public or explicitly approved reusable material that is relevant to the task.

categories.label: Pause and check
categories.description: Material whose ownership, markings, contract terms, privacy, or approved purpose requires confirmation.

categories.label: Restricted
categories.description: Secrets, classified material, controlled technical data, or other content outside this workflow.

items.detail: The notice is published on an official public website and contains no submission-restricted attachment.
items.feedback: Ready for this exercise. Preserve the source URL and publication date so claims remain traceable.

items.detail: The content owner labeled it for reuse in unclassified business development materials.
items.feedback: Ready for the stated purpose, subject to current version and access checks.

items.detail: The email discusses acquisition priorities and has no clear reuse authorization.
items.feedback: Pause and check with the designated capture, Contracts, and information-handling owners. Do not infer permission from access.

items.detail: A teammate suggests removing the title block and uploading the drawing.
items.feedback: Restricted in this workflow. Removing a marking does not change handling requirements or authorize use.

items.detail: The model would need a teammate's password to retrieve an attachment.
items.feedback: Restricted. Never place credentials or access tokens in prompts. Use authorized systems and individual access.

items.detail: The brief only needs an aggregate statement about team certifications.
items.feedback: Pause. The personal details are unnecessary. Use an approved aggregate or sanitized capability statement.

practice.debrief: Access is not authorization. Verify the tool, data, purpose, markings, contract or program restrictions, and minimum necessary content before use.

quiz.prompt: An AI tool is enterprise-approved. What else must be true before using program data?

options.text: Nothing; tool approval covers every dataset and purpose.
options.feedback: General tool approval does not override data, contract, customer, program, privacy, or access restrictions.

options.text: The data type, purpose, access, and program-specific rules also permit the use.
options.feedback: Correct. Approval must fit the complete use case, not only the tool name.

options.text: A coworker has already tried it once.
options.feedback: Prior use by a coworker is not evidence of authorization.

quiz.explanation: Responsible input design checks authorization across the tool, information, purpose, people, and governing workflow.

quiz.prompt: A source has an unclear handling marking. What is the appropriate next step?

options.text: Remove the marking and proceed.
options.feedback: Users may not remove a marking to create permission.

options.text: Guess based on similar documents.
options.feedback: Similar appearance does not establish the handling rule for this source.

options.text: Pause and ask the designated security, contracts, legal, export, privacy, or program owner.
options.feedback: Correct. Route uncertainty to the authorized owner rather than interpreting it yourself.

quiz.explanation: Escalation is a productive control when the learner lacks authority or the rules are unclear.

quiz.prompt: Which source is preferable for an early, non-customer solution concept?

options.text: A public requirement and current, approved reusable capability content
options.feedback: Correct. These sources can support early work while preserving provenance and approved reuse boundaries.

options.text: A competitor's proprietary proposal obtained from an old shared drive
options.feedback: Do not use material with unclear or improper ownership. Route the discovery appropriately.

options.text: Controlled technical data with labels removed
options.feedback: Removing labels does not remove restrictions or create authorization.

quiz.explanation: Select the least sensitive source set that is authorized and sufficient for the task.

takeaway: Tool approval is only one gate. Confirm data, purpose, access, program rules, and minimum necessary content together.

title: Orchestrate a structured AI workflow
description: Connect bounded AI tasks through schemas, checkpoints, and explicit fallbacks instead of relying on one long prompt.
outcome: You can design a multi-step workflow whose intermediate artifacts are visible and testable.
objectives: Create structured intermediate outputs that later steps can consume safely.
Insert validation and human approval between dependent tasks.
Define stop conditions for missing, conflicting, or unauthorized information.

concepts.title: Artifacts create control
concepts.body: A source register, fact table, issue log, and draft are easier to review than a hidden chain of model reasoning. Ask for observable artifacts with stable fields.

concepts.title: Gates belong between dependencies
concepts.body: Review the artifact that a later task depends on before passing it forward. The higher the consequence, the stronger the gate.

concepts.title: Fallbacks are part of the design
concepts.body: A robust workflow states what happens when a source is missing, facts conflict, the model cannot cite support, or policy blocks the next step.

practice.title: Design a reviewable monthly program brief
instructions: Use the fictional approved source notes to define the workflow.
Specify intermediate artifacts, human gates, and stop conditions.
Require the final brief to preserve source IDs and uncertainty.
practice.scenario: A program office wants a repeatable workflow for a monthly leadership brief. The training data is fictional and sanitized. Program leadership, engineering, finance, and contracts retain their existing approval roles.
sourceNotes: S1 schedule extract: Integration event is forecast for October 18.
S2 risk register: Authentication dependency is rated medium and has an owner.
S3 engineering note: Interface test passed 17 of 18 approved cases; one case remains under review.
S4 finance summary: Current estimate is within the approved planning range.
S5 action log: Customer decision on the test window is due September 30.
No source authorizes a contract change or a final technical conclusion.

fields.label: Intermediate artifacts
fields.prompt: What structured outputs should the workflow create?
fields.placeholder: Source register, fact table with source IDs, conflict log, draft brief

fields.label: Review gates
fields.prompt: Who validates each artifact before the next step?
fields.placeholder: Functional owners validate facts; program manager approves the final brief

fields.label: Stop conditions
fields.prompt: When must the workflow pause instead of completing?
fields.placeholder: Missing source, unresolved conflict, unsupported conclusion, policy concern

fields.label: Output schema
fields.prompt: What fields make the final brief consistent and traceable?
fields.placeholder: Status, evidence, source IDs, owner, decision needed, due date, uncertainty

successChecks: Every final claim points to a validated intermediate artifact and source ID.
Functional owners validate facts in their areas.
The workflow stops on unresolved conflicts or missing authority.
The final brief separates status, risk, decision, and uncertainty.
practice.modelAnswer: Step 1: Create a source register with source ID, owner, date, approved use, and version. Stop if a source is not approved. Step 2: Extract a fact table with exact support and no conclusions; functional owners validate their rows. Step 3: Compare facts and create a conflict and gap log. Stop on unresolved material conflicts. Step 4: Draft the brief from validated rows only, using status, evidence and source IDs, decision needed, owner, due date, and uncertainty fields. Step 5: Program leadership reviews the complete brief; no output changes technical, financial, or contractual authority.

quiz.prompt: Why request a structured fact table before asking for a final brief?

options.text: It exposes the evidence and creates a reviewable input for later drafting.
options.feedback: Correct. Visible intermediate artifacts improve traceability and error control.

options.text: It guarantees the model cannot make an error.
options.feedback: Structure reduces risk but does not eliminate model or source errors.

options.text: It transfers approval authority to the workflow.
options.feedback: Workflow structure does not change organizational authority.

quiz.explanation: Structured artifacts create inspectable seams between dependent tasks.

quiz.prompt: Two approved sources conflict on a milestone date. What should the workflow do?

options.text: Choose the earlier date without noting the conflict.
options.feedback: A silent choice can create a false statement and hide a decision that needs an owner.

options.text: Record the conflict, pause the affected claim, and route it to the source owners.
options.feedback: Correct. The workflow should preserve uncertainty and obtain an authorized resolution.

options.text: Average the two dates.
options.feedback: Averaging dates has no evidentiary basis and may create a third incorrect value.

quiz.explanation: Stop conditions protect the workflow from converting ambiguity into false certainty.

quiz.prompt: What makes an intermediate artifact reusable across runs?

options.text: Stable fields, source provenance, version information, and an acceptance check
options.feedback: Correct. These features support consistent review and safe handoff.

options.text: A hidden format that only the original author understands
options.feedback: Hidden conventions weaken maintainability and review.

options.text: Removing dates so the artifact never appears old
options.feedback: Version and date information are essential for recency and change control.

quiz.explanation: Reusable artifacts have explicit schemas, provenance, versioning, and quality criteria.

takeaway: Design the chain, not just the prompt: visible artifacts, source IDs, human gates, and clear stop conditions.

title: Reconcile evidence across sources
description: Compare source authority, recency, scope, and conflict before an AI-generated claim reaches a decision-maker.
outcome: You can build a claim-to-source matrix and route interpretation questions to authorized reviewers.
objectives: Trace each consequential claim to one or more approved sources.
Evaluate conflicts using authority, scope, date, and version rather than model confidence.
Separate factual comparison from legal, contractual, or technical interpretation.

concepts.title: Source quality is claim-specific
concepts.body: A source may be authoritative for one field and irrelevant for another. A schedule can show the current plan, while an executed contract document governs a contractual requirement.

concepts.title: Conflict needs a disposition
concepts.body: Do not ask AI to hide or vote on conflicting sources. Record the conflict, affected claim, source owners, and required resolution.

concepts.title: Comparison is not interpretation
concepts.body: AI can point out text differences in approved documents. Authorized Contracts, Legal, Compliance, Engineering, Security, or program officials determine what those differences mean. This training is not legal advice.

practice.title: Audit a contractual milestone summary
instructions: Compare the AI draft with the fictional source pack.
Classify each claim based only on the supplied evidence.
Route interpretation and change questions to the appropriate authorized owners.
practice.scenario: A program analyst used AI to summarize fictional, sanitized program documents. Leadership will use the brief for planning. The exercise tests evidence handling and does not provide contractual or legal advice.
sourcePack: S1 executed statement of work: The design review is due 30 calendar days after kickoff.
S2 kickoff record: Kickoff occurred September 18.
S3 current integrated schedule: Internal target for the design review is October 11.
S4 program note: The team wants extra margin before the due date.
S5 draft modification: Proposes moving the review to October 25; status is not executed.
S6 compliance matrix: Deliverable A002 requires program and Contracts review before submission.
practice.draft: The customer changed the contractual design review date to October 11 and approved the draft modification. Missing that date automatically creates a financial penalty. Deliverable A002 can be submitted directly by the analyst.

claims.text: October 11 is the current internal target.
claims.feedback: Supported by S3 as an internal planning target. Do not relabel it as a contractual date.

claims.text: The customer changed the contractual date to October 11.
claims.feedback: No supplied source states that. S3 is an internal schedule, not an executed change.
S5 explicitly says the modification is not executed.

claims.text: Missing October 11 automatically creates a financial penalty.
claims.feedback: No source supports this claim. Any contractual or legal implication must be routed to authorized Contracts or Legal reviewers.

claims.text: The analyst may submit A002 without further review.
claims.feedback: S6 requires program and Contracts review before submission.

claims.text: The executed statement of work defines the due date relative to kickoff.
claims.feedback: The relationship is supported by S1 and S2, but an authorized reviewer should confirm the calendar calculation and any governing terms before external use.

practice.improvedDraft: The current internal target for the design review is October 11 (S3), intended to provide margin. The executed statement of work states a due date of 30 calendar days after the September 18 kickoff (S1, S2); Contracts and program leadership should confirm the applicable date and calculation before external use. A draft modification proposes October 25 but is not executed (S5). No supplied source establishes an automatic financial penalty. Deliverable A002 requires program and Contracts review before submission (S6).

quiz.prompt: A current schedule and an executed contract document show different dates. What is the best AI-assisted response?

options.text: Report the schedule date as contractual because it is newer.
options.feedback: Recency alone does not make a planning source authoritative for a contractual claim.

options.text: Record both dates and their source roles, then route the conflict to authorized program and Contracts owners.
options.feedback: Correct. Preserve the evidence and obtain an authorized disposition.

options.text: Ask AI to choose whichever date seems reasonable.
options.feedback: Model judgment cannot resolve source authority or create a contract interpretation.

quiz.explanation: Source authority depends on the claim. Conflicts must remain visible until the proper owner resolves them.

quiz.prompt: What belongs in a claim-to-source matrix?

options.text: Claim, source ID, exact support, version or date, confidence limits, and reviewer status
options.feedback: Correct. These fields let a reviewer trace and evaluate the claim.

options.text: Only the final prose and a model confidence score
options.feedback: Model confidence does not replace evidence or provenance.

options.text: A list of sources without mapping them to claims
options.feedback: A bibliography alone does not show which source supports which statement.

quiz.explanation: Verification is strongest when it connects each consequential claim to specific evidence and review state.

quiz.prompt: AI highlights a difference between two clauses. Who determines the legal or contractual meaning?

options.text: The model with the longest answer
options.feedback: Length does not create authority or legal reliability.

options.text: Any user who can access both documents
options.feedback: Access does not grant interpretation or decision authority.

options.text: The designated authorized Contracts or Legal reviewer, with relevant program context
options.feedback: Correct. AI may support comparison, but authorized professionals own interpretation.

quiz.explanation: AI-assisted document comparison does not replace qualified, authorized review.

takeaway: Map claims to sources, expose conflicts, and route interpretation to the people who hold the authority.

title: Build reusable team handoffs
description: Package prompts, sources, checks, exceptions, and approvals so another qualified teammate can repeat the work safely.
outcome: You can turn a useful one-time AI workflow into a versioned, reviewable team playbook.
objectives: Document purpose, approved inputs, output schema, controls, and ownership.
Capture exceptions and failure modes without retaining sensitive prompt content.
Define when the playbook must be reviewed, updated, or retired.

concepts.title: Reuse the control pattern
concepts.body: A reusable asset is more than a saved prompt. It includes approved source rules, review steps, expected output fields, examples, stop conditions, and owners.

concepts.title: Version the workflow
concepts.body: Record the owner, version, approval date, and next review. A playbook can become unsafe when policies, tools, programs, or source formats change.

concepts.title: Preserve lessons, not sensitive history
concepts.body: Capture generalized failures and improvements. Do not store personal, proprietary, controlled, classified, or customer-sensitive prompt histories in the playbook.

practice.title: Convert a mission-support brief into a safe repeatable process
instructions: Review the draft handoff and identify what a second operator would need.
Define the checks, owners, and change-control information.
Compare your plan with the reusable model plan.
practice.scenario: A mission-support team has a useful weekly brief workflow built with fictional sanitized data. A second shift wants to adopt it. Existing operational and security procedures remain controlling.
practice.aiDraft: Paste the weekly notes into AI and ask for the same brief as last time. The old chat has the format. If a number is missing, let the model estimate it so the brief stays complete.

concerns.text: The handoff does not define approved source types or prohibited content.
The required format exists only in an old chat and has no controlled version.
The workflow invites unsupported estimates to appear as facts.
No person validates the brief or owns updates to the workflow.

planPrompts.label: Purpose and inputs
planPrompts.placeholder: State the approved use, permitted source set, prohibited content, and data-minimization rules...

planPrompts.label: Process and checks
planPrompts.placeholder: Define the template, source mapping, missing-data behavior, and reviewer checklist...

planPrompts.label: Owners and approvals
planPrompts.placeholder: Name the workflow owner, brief approver, functional reviewers, and escalation path...

planPrompts.label: Version and change
planPrompts.placeholder: Record version, approval date, known limitations, review trigger, and retirement criteria...

modelPlan: Publish a versioned purpose statement and list approved source types, prohibited information, tool boundaries, and the controlling procedures.
Provide a clean prompt template and output schema outside chat history. Require source IDs and [NEEDS INPUT] for missing facts.
Add functional fact checks and a named mission-support approver before distribution.
Document common failures using sanitized examples, plus stop and escalation conditions.
Assign a playbook owner, approval date, next review, and triggers such as tool, policy, program, or source-format changes.

quiz.prompt: What turns a saved prompt into a responsible team playbook?

options.text: Approved-use boundaries, source rules, checks, owners, stop conditions, and versioning
options.feedback: Correct. Reuse depends on the surrounding control system, not only prompt wording.

options.text: A note that says the prompt worked once
options.feedback: One successful run does not establish repeatability, safety, or continued approval.

options.text: A copy of every historical prompt and source
options.feedback: Historical content may be sensitive, outdated, or misleading. Preserve generalized lessons and approved examples.

quiz.explanation: A playbook makes the safe operating conditions and human responsibilities repeatable.

quiz.prompt: When should a team review an AI workflow playbook?

options.text: Only after a serious incident
options.feedback: Incident review matters, but waiting for harm is not sufficient change control.

options.text: On a scheduled cadence and when tools, policies, programs, sources, owners, or risks change
options.feedback: Correct. Both periodic and event-driven reviews keep the playbook current.

options.text: Never, if the prompt text stays the same
options.feedback: The environment around an unchanged prompt can make its use outdated or unsafe.

quiz.explanation: Versioned workflows need lifecycle ownership, not a one-time approval.

quiz.prompt: What should a reusable workflow do when a required fact is missing?

options.text: Estimate it silently to preserve the format.
options.feedback: A silent estimate can become a false operational claim.

options.text: Reuse the value from the previous period without checking.
options.feedback: Prior-period data may be stale and should not be substituted without an authorized rule.

options.text: Mark the gap, stop the affected claim, and route it to the source owner.
options.feedback: Correct. The workflow should make missing information actionable and visible.

quiz.explanation: A repeatable fallback protects integrity when normal inputs are incomplete.

takeaway: Reuse a versioned operating pattern with inputs, checks, stops, and owners, not a chat transcript.
